blocks.text: that is, they were flowing. Second, by the name נופת nopheth, which means distillation, since נוף nuph is a verb meaning to drip or to sprinkle. Thus in Psal. XIX, 11. נופת צופים is the distillation of honeycombs. And in Cant. IV, 11. נופת תטפנה, Your lips drip distillation. And in Prov. V, 3. The lips of a harlot drip distillation. So also Prov. XXIV, 13. ונופת, And distillation is sweet to your palate. And Prov. XXVII, 7. The sated soul tramples נופת, the dripping, supply of honey or of honeycombs. For this is to be supplied everywhere. Third, from the verb צוף, that is, to flow, צוף tsuph is the name of a honeycomb, properly a flowing one. Thus Prov. XVI, 24. צוף דבש, pleasant words are a honeycomb (a flowing one). And Psal. XIX, 11. The judgments of the Lord are sweeter than honey, ונופת צופים, and than the distillation of honeycombs (flowing ones). Fourth, the verb רדה rada, which the Hebrews render to take, the Syrians in Iud. XIV, 9., following the idiom of their own language, refer to the flowing of honey, because for them ܢܕܼ means to flow. So these words about the honey found by Samson, וירדהו אל כפיו, And he took it into his hands, are rendered thus by the Syriac translator: ܘܢܕܼ ܗܘܐ ܕܒܫܐ ܥܠ ܐܝܕܘܗܝ ܘܡܗܠܟ And the honey flowed down over his hands, and he went on. And again in the same verse, He did not tell them that he had רדה הדבש, taken the honey, from the body of the lion. So the Hebrews; but the Syrians have ܢܕܼ ܕܒܫܐ, the honey had flowed: as in 1 Sam. XIV, 25. (or 26.) ܘܢܕܼ ܗܘܐ ܕܒܫܐ And that honey was flowing. Fifth, in the same place the flowing of honey is, in the Chaldee, בריז דובשא. For برز [baraza] baraza in Arabic is to go out. Hence בריז brez, or briz, in Chaldee is the flow of honey going out from the comb. To this perhaps belongs the fact that the inventor of honey, Bacchus, was called Brisaeus or Bressaeus. Cornutus on Persius, Satire 1: Father Liber is surnamed BRISAEUS from the use of honey, because he himself is said to have first discovered honey and to press it from the combs (read to have pressed). Hesychius: Βρησσαῖος· Διόνυσος [Brēssaios; Dionysos]. To the same point is the fact that they called Brisae the Nymphs who taught Aristaeus [col. 521] the method of making honey. Heraclides in the Constitution of the Coans, or rather of the Ceans: Ἀρισταῖον δέ φασι μαθεῖν παρὰ Βρισσῶν τὴν μελιττουργίαν [Aristaion de phasi mathein para Brissōn tēn melittourgian]. The Etymologicum: Βρίσαι· Νύμφαι οὕτω καλουμέναι [Brisai; Nymphai houtō kaloumenai]. And immediately after: Μελιττουργίαν αὐταὶ τὸν Ἀρισταῖον ἐδίδαξαν [Melittourgian autai ton Aristaion edidaxan].

[III, 381] It has been proved so far that honey abounded in Judaea and was produced plentifully, even in the fields and woods. Why, then, could it not have been used as food by John the Baptist? To many, ordinary honey seems too luxurious a food to have suited John in such abstinence. Accordingly they hold that the wild honey of which the Evangelists speak was bitter and altogether unpleasant to the taste. Thus Isidore of Pelusium, Epistle 132, defines it as μέλι ὄρειον, ὑπὸ μελισσῶν ἀγρίων γινόμενον, πικρότατον, καὶ πάσῃ γεύσει πολέμιον [meli oreion, hypo melissōn agriōn ginomenon, pikrotaton, kai pasē geusei polemion]. And Euthymius says: Wild honey is made by wild bees in the clefts of rocks; but it is bitter and unpleasant. But these things are said without grounds, and do not agree well with Scripture, which would not so greatly commend Judaea for its honey if the honey produced in the fields were unpleasant and bitter. I am not unaware that in certain places bitter honey is produced, for example the Sardinian and the Corsican, whether the cause lies in the wormwood on which the bees feed (Dioscorides, book 2: Τὸ δὲ ἐν Σαρδονίᾳ γενώμενον μέλι πικρὸν διὰ τὴν τοῦ ἀψινθίου νομήν [To de en Sardonia genōmenon meli pikron dia tēn tou apsinthiou nomēn]; Galen, On the Simple Faculty of Medicines, book 7: If any honey is bitter, as the Sardinian, it is clear that it too is of a mixed faculty, as if one of us had mixed wormwood into it); or whether it comes from the box tree, which is very abundant in Corsica (Diodorus, book 5: Φύεται δὲ κατὰ τὴν νῆσον ταύτην καὶ πύξος πλείστη, καὶ διάφορος· δι’ ἣν καὶ τὸ μέλι τὸ γινόμενον ἐν αὐτῇ παντελῶς γίνεται πικρόν [Phyetai de kata tēn nēson tautēn kai pyxos pleistē, kai diaphoros; di’ hēn kai to meli to ginomenon en autē pantelōs ginetai pikron]); or from yews, as these lines of the poet suggest, in Eclogue 5:
So may your swarms shun the Cyrnean yews.

On which Servius: The yew is a poisonous tree, which abounds in Corsica. Likewise: Cyrenean yews, fed on which bees make a most bitter honey. Or from feeding on hemlock, as Ovid writes of wax in the Amores, book 1, Elegy 12:
Which, I think, the Corsican bee sent, gathered from afar from the hemlock flower, under infamous honey.
Or from thyme of bad flavour, as Martial, book 11, Epigram 13:
You bid Hyblaean or Hymettian honey to be born for you, and you set Corsican thyme before the Cecropian bee.
